prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation by bifunctional degraders that recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins
for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: Both parts turn a biological process into a designable chemical reaction and have changed what researchers and clinicians can actually do. Degraders (PROTACs) make proximity to an E3 ligase a rational design principle for small molecules and open targets that inhibitors cannot reach. Base editors are engineered deaminases that rewrite single nucleotides chemically, without double-strand breaks, and are already in clinical use. They are distinct achievements: one is a pharmacological modality, the other a tool for precise chemistry on the genome. Together they give a coherent chemical-biology prize built on molecular design, with a clear line from mechanism to application.
statement.case_against: Neither part is free of timing and novelty problems. No PROTAC drug is approved, and base editing arrives six years after the 2020 CRISPR chemistry prize, so a sceptical member can call it a follow-on. Pairing two fashionable chemical-biology topics could also read as a medicine prize in disguise, and by narrowing both fields to three names it leaves out Handa, Ciulli, Gray and the Japanese cytidine-deaminase work. A mature, plainly chemical alternative such as sequencing by synthesis may be the safer choice.

responses.point: Chabes ranks degradation first and wants Crews, Deshaies and Handa, so the PROTAC and the molecular-glue (cereblon) arms are both recognised, with maturity judged adequate because many groups have reproduced it and drugs are in the clinic.
responses.response: I agree on first-rank merit, since induced proximity is the principle I would most want to see rewarded. I part with him on Handa. Cereblon explains why thalidomide-type drugs work, but the glue arm is a mechanism discovery, while the design logic that generalises is the bifunctional degrader. Including Handa also uses a place I would rather give to a second achievement. If the committee feels that the glue story cannot be left out, I would accept Handa in place of Deshaies, and I would not defend this boundary strongly.

responses.point: Aqvist puts sequencing by synthesis first as a fully mature, chemistry-driven invention by Balasubramanian and Klenerman, and he supports Liu alone on base editing as the clear intellectual driver.
responses.response: I take his maturity argument seriously, and that is why B011 stays among my alternatives. Where I disagree is on Liu alone for base editing. Kondo and Nishida reported deaminase-based cytidine editing independently at about the same time, so excluding them is a credit judgement, not a settled fact. I still favour Liu in my configuration because the cytosine and adenine editors and their systematic engineering are his group's work. I would like to hear from him whether Target-AID changes his view.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sequencing first for its clean physical principle and portable long-read capability, and he flags that some key candidates may be deceased, which would limit who can be credited.
responses.response: I accept that nanopore sensing is original and mature, and it is the biosensing field I know best. My reservation is attribution: it is split across several groups, and a prize needs living, identifiable laureates. If Branton or Bayley cannot be named, the remaining configuration looks thin, so I rank it below degradation. I would be glad to be corrected on the status of those candidates, since I cannot verify it from the files.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range protein electron transfer first, as a quantitative physical mechanism for bioenergetics that has been confirmed for decades and is arguably overdue.
responses.response: This is a fair point and I do not dispute the standard of the science. For me the question is whether the work changed what others can do. Electron-transfer rules are foundational and textbook material, but they have not given chemists a new tool or modality in the way degraders or base editors have. I would not oppose it as a second part, but I cannot place it above my preferred pairing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees base editing as distinct enough from the 2020 CRISPR prize.
Whether the PROTAC credit should include Handa for the molecular-glue strand, and how to weigh Ciulli, Sakamoto, Gray and Ito.
Whether the lack of an approved degrader makes B034 premature compared with mature candidates such as B011.
Whether the Kondo and Nishida independent cytidine-editing work deserves a place beside Liu.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I am a bioengineering and biosensor researcher at Linkoping, and none of my mentors or collaborators (Stevens, Boey) appear among the credited names. Brief note: Emma Sparr's research overlap is not a conflict for any shortlisted candidate.
